items.X_name: Future-reader orientation
items.X_desc: On a 0–10 scale, score the extent to which the answer is framed for a general future reader through definitions, broad context, analogies, or multiple cases rather than only the asker's immediate setup; do not judge whether this orientation is beneficial.
items.Y_desc: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the answer generalizes beyond the immediate problem through reusable methods, broader context, alternatives, or definitions; do not judge whether that orientation is good.

items.X_name: Hint mode: deliberate withholding of the completed solution
items.X_desc: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer withholds the finish rather than carrying the work to a conclusion: an explicit 'Hint:' or 'HINT:' opener, a numbered ladder of sub-steps for the reader to perform ('Show that...', 'Apply (1) and (2)'), a closing interrogative aimed at the reader ('Which terms are that?', 'Does that make sense?', 'can you show that'), an explicit handoff ('I leave it you to simplify this expression', 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'), or a stated final substitution left unevaluated. 0 = the answer runs to a complete finished result with nothing left for the reader; 5 = mostly complete but ends with one open prompt; 10 = the answer is a bare hint or scaffold with the substantive work explicitly deferred. Score only how much is withheld and how explicitly. You must NOT judge whether withholding is pedagogically good, nor whether the hint points in the right direction.
items.Y_desc: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the answer deliberately stops short and hands the remaining work back to the reader. Traces to count: an explicit hint label opening the post, in any casing; a numbered programme of things the reader is told to 'show' or 'prove' themselves; explicit statements that the remainder is left to the reader or that the reader should now simplify, finish, or figure out what happens next; a closing question put back to the reader; a final line that names the next step without taking it. Score LOW when the argument is carried all the way to a stated conclusion or final value. 0 = complete worked argument ending in its conclusion; 10 = nothing but a pointer or opening move with the work explicitly delegated. You MUST NOT judge whether hinting is pedagogically right or whether a full solution is better; score only how much of the work is withheld.

items.X_name: Language presupposing that sibling answers already exist
items.X_desc: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer's own wording presupposes that other answers or comments to the same question are already present: naming another answerer or user, phrases such as 'To expand on X's answer', 'As was pointed out in another answer', 'as mentioned before', 'this is nicely considered in the answer from ...', 'I see I've just repeated someone's comment', positioning itself as an alternative or supplement ('A worse way to prove this is...', 'For the sake of interest'), or engaging an argument that is not in the question text. 0 = the answer engages the raw question from scratch as if nothing had yet been said; 5 = one glancing phrase implying prior discussion; 10 = the answer is structured explicitly as a reply to or extension of another answer and cannot stand alone. Score only the presence of this presupposing language. You must NOT judge whether the supplement is valuable or whether the engagement is fair.
items.Y_name: Presupposition that other answers already exist
items.Y_desc: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the wording presupposes that other answers, or prior discussion of this same question, already exist at the moment of writing. Count constructions such as: explicit reference to another answer or to what was 'pointed out', 'mentioned', or 'said' before; offers of an alternative, shorter, or supplementary route ('a bit shorter', 'to expand on', 'for the sake of interest', 'another way'); deferral of a sub-case to someone else's treatment; corrections or qualifications aimed at a prior posted argument rather than at the question itself. 0 = the text engages the raw question completely from scratch, with no linguistic sign that anything has yet been said; 5 = one passing gesture toward prior material; 10 = the answer is framed throughout as an addition, correction, or alternative to material already present. You MUST NOT judge whether referring to prior answers is gracious, redundant, helpful, or correct, and you must not judge answer quality in any way. Score only how much of this presupposition is textually present.

items.X_name: Hedged first-person stance versus flat declarative assertion
items.X_desc: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of epistemic hedging in the answer's voice: first-person uncertainty markers ('I think', 'I'm not sure', 'I would do something like that', 'I believe', 'no promise that they will be helpful', 'may not be optimal'), softening discourse openers ('Well', 'It is not quite clear', 'something like'), conditional framing of the author's own claims, and explicit confessions of incomplete knowledge. Score 0 when the answer is uniformly flat and declarative with no first-person qualification at all, 5 when there is one clear hedge in an otherwise assertive text, and 10 when hedging saturates the answer from the first clause onward. Score only the density of the hedging language. You must NOT judge whether the hedging is warranted, honest, or well calibrated, and you must NOT judge whether the assertions are true.
items.Y_name: Flat declarative assertion versus epistemic hedging
items.Y_desc: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT of flat, unhedged declarative assertion, scoring the hedged pole low. Score HIGH for: verdicts delivered as bare single words or single sentences before any argument; assertions with no epistemic qualifier; 'it is clear', 'it is easy to check', 'of course', 'obviously', 'we are done'. Score LOW for: first-person uncertainty ('I think', 'I'm not sure', 'I suppose', 'I believe', 'maybe'), self-deprecation about the author's own contribution, scare-quoted disclaimers that the treatment is only intuitive or non-rigorous, apologies, expressions of doubt about whether the reader already knew this, and closing pleasantries that solicit approval. 0 = pervasively hedged and tentative; 10 = flatly declarative throughout. You MUST NOT judge whether the confidence is warranted, whether the claims are correct, or whether hedging is honest; score only the register.

items.X_name: Era-marked notation, markup vintage and venue conventions
items.X_desc: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of vintage or off-convention presentation habits that mark an answer as belonging to an older or non-current stratum of the site's conventions: mathematics typed as literal unicode or plain characters in running prose rather than in math delimiters ('k≥2', '⇒', 'N-1'), ASCII exponent and function notation ('t^(3/2)', 'cot^{-1}' typed outside math mode), regionally or historically marked abbreviations ('hcf' rather than 'gcd'), quoted-string state names in prose ('on'/'off' with typographic quotes), subject matter tied to a bygone teaching practice discussed as such, and absence of the structural markup (lists, display blocks, blockquotes) that is now routine. 0 = fully current, uniformly delimited, structurally marked-up presentation; 5 = a mix of current markup with a few plain-text mathematical expressions; 10 = the whole answer uses out-of-convention plain-text mathematics and vocabulary. Score only the vintage of the surface conventions. You must NOT judge whether the conventions are better or worse, and you must NOT infer or state any date.
items.Y_name: Vintage of notation and markup conventions
items.Y_desc: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the mathematical notation and markup look like an older vintage of this site's conventions rather than current practice. Traces to count: mathematics typed as plain ASCII with no math delimiters at all (things like t^(3/2), >=, x^2 written bare in prose); raw Unicode operator and arrow glyphs pasted inline where a markup macro would now be used; abbreviated blackboard-bold and older macro spellings rather than their long modern forms; older combinatorial and number-theoretic shorthands (pre-superscript binomial forms, 'hcf' rather than 'gcd', subfactorial written with a leading bang); a single undifferentiated display block where a modern post would use an aligned multi-line environment; prose typographic habits such as double-dot ellipses, spaces before punctuation, or emoticons. 0 = uniformly current, environment-rich markup; 10 = heavily dated or markup-free throughout. You MUST NOT judge whether the notation is clear, correct, or good; score only how much dated-convention texture is present.

items.X_name: Bulk and exposition scale of the answer

Count what is on the page. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the extra material is useful, or whether the answer is correct, complete or well written; a long wrong answer and a long right answer receive the same score.
items.Y_name: Bulk: overall length and count of display blocks

Calibrate so that 0 = a single sentence or a single line of mathematics with essentially no prose; 3 = one short paragraph plus one display; 6 = several paragraphs with three to five displays; 10 = many screens of prose interleaved with numerous displays, tables, or enumerated case sections. You MUST NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the answer is padded, or whether it is admirably concise. Score only the amount of material present.
